extracted.intended_audience: cartoonists and comics creators (aspiring and experienced)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and composing a comics page: panel layout, page flow, pacing, and thumbnail planning to control reader attention and narrative timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page flow (left-to-right, top-to-bottom)
rubrics_metrics.description: In this culture, we read them left to right and top to bottom. Cartoonists always need to keep this knowledge at the front of their brain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design pages to lead the reader’s eye in the direction it wants to go — i.e., “go with the flow.” If panel composition goes against page flow it can jar the reading experience; use that effect deliberately only when you want to stop or shock the reader. Example: Jaime Hernandez arranges panels and figure direction to guide the eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition directs attention ('secret messages')
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel design sends secret messages to your brain telling it 'look here'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use character orientation, gaze, and compositional lines to point the reader toward the next beat or focal element (e.g., the protagonist is pointed in the direction of page flow). These cues subtly control eye movement and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel as sentence; tier as paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: The most basic element of the comics page is the panel (like a sentence). A horizontal row of panels is called a tier (like a paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat a new tier like the start of a new idea: use tier breaks to signal changes in time, location, or narrative emphasis. The post notes specific tier breaks marking major changes (panels 4 and 7 in the example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing via panel repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Panel repetition is a simple way to stretch time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add repeated panels/extra beats to slow down a moment and lengthen perceived time. The post references Scott McCloud examples where inserting extra beats changes the timing of a response and stretches narrative time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pacing and emphasis via panel size and grid manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Playing with panel size changes how time is felt and gives moments significance; a big panel equals a big moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare a perfect grid (every panel same size) versus varied panel sizes: grids create uniform rhythm; changing sizes alters tempo and emphasis. Use larger panels to indicate importance or a 'pregnant pause'; smaller or repeated panels to slow or quicken beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thumbnails as blueprints and problem-solving tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Thumbnails are rough preliminary sketches — not about creating artwork, it's about recording information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch thumbnails to plan page flow, pacing, and composition before committing to finished art. Treat thumbnails as problem-solving: scribble, iterate, and refine layout until it works. Don't be too precious about thumbnails; they exist to let you test solutions (example: thumbnails and finished art for Satchel Page).
